settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: doNormalize removes null bytes via failIfNullBytePresent (line 355), matching the documented behavior, so the null-byte portion is guarded.

getPrefixLength rejects a leading ':' (lines 639-640) and rejects a letter-colon sequence that is followed by a non-separator/out-of-range char (lines 666-669), which blocks a number of colon-based names.
normalize/normalizeNoEndSeparator are pure string helpers; they do not themselves open, read, write, or delete files, so no sink is reachable inside this source.
The '..'-escape case for genuinely relative names returns null (lines 411-413), which is the documented invalid-path behavior.
candidates.description: FilenameUtils.normalize(String) / normalize(String, boolean) delegate to doNormalize(char separator, boolean keepSeparator) (lines 196-198, 243-246, 290-292, 337-340). doNormalize first computes prefix = getPrefixLength(fileName) and returns null only if prefix < 0 (lines 361-364). getPrefixLength (lines 630-683) always recognizes Windows-style prefixes regardless of host OS: a leading ':' returns NOT_FOUND (639-640), but any first char followed by ':' where the char is A-Z (upper-cased) is treated as a drive prefix returning 2 or 3 (lines 658-665), and a leading pair of separators is treated as a UNC prefix (lines 671-679). The class javadoc explicitly notes both prefix styles are matched on every machine (lines 60-76). Consequently, inputs such as "C:/.." style names, or names whose first character is a letter/dot/other non-'/' followed by ':', acquire a non-zero prefix on a POSIX host, and the ".."-collapsing loop (lines 406-431) will remove the '..' segment relative to that prefix instead of returning null. The document/output is then returned with a Windows-flavored prefix rather than being flagged invalid. The javadoc contracts also promise null "if invalid" and that null bytes are removed (lines 193-194, 287-289); null-byte handling is actually enforced by failIfNullBytePresent(fileName) at line 355, so that specific old issue is guarded here. Root cause: OS-independent prefix detection in getPrefixLength combined with doNormalize trusting that prefix to bound '..' resolution. Preconditions to matter: an application on a non-Windows host must pass attacker-influenced text to FilenameUtils.normalize/normalizeNoEndSeparator and then use the returned value as a filesystem path; the library itself performs no file I/O here. Impact cannot be established from this repository alone because the caller/usage is absent. Counter-evidence: getPrefixLength was explicitly hardened by IO-483 (changes.xml lines 104-105; leading ':' rejected at lines 639-640, embedded invalid colon rejected at 666-669) and normalize is documented to return null for invalid names; FileUtils.resolveFile/canonical-path checks elsewhere in the project are the normal containment mechanism, and I did not read them. This is a candidate, not a confirmed traversal vulnerability.
missing_evidence: No caller of FilenameUtils.normalize* exists in this repository, so reachability from an untrusted input source to a file operation is unproven.
FileUtils.resolveFile / canonical-path containment logic that most consumers would use was not inspected, so it is unknown whether it compensates for the prefix behavior.
No test or documentation in the inspected files demonstrates exploitation using a POSIX host with a drive/UNC-prefixed name; behavior was reasoned from code, not executed.
preconditions: Application runs on a non-Windows (POSIX) host.
Untrusted or attacker-influenced text is passed to FilenameUtils.normalize() / normalizeNoEndSeparator() (possibly with unixSeparator=true).
The returned normalized string is subsequently used by the caller as a filesystem path (no such use exists inside this library source I read).
The name contains a character sequence that getPrefixLength classifies as a Windows drive or UNC prefix (e.g. an embedded ':' after a letter).
candidates.title: FilenameUtils.normalize treats Windows drive/UNC prefixes as absolute even on Unix, so a POSIX-callable path containing an embedded colon is not rejected as escaping
